title: How to work a long arm cross-stitch
subtitle: An elongated X for textured fills and traditional samplers
excerpt: Long arm cross-stitch is a variation on the full cross where one diagonal is worked over two squares instead of one, giving the stitch a deliberate asymmetry. It covers fabric faster than a standard full cross and gives a braided or woven texture to a filled area.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, cross-stitch variations. The long arm cross is documented in sampler traditions from the 17th century onward.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cross-stitch variation where one diagonal is worked over two squares and the return diagonal is worked over one square, giving the stitch an asymmetric elongated shape and a braided texture in filled areas.

Two diagonal stitches worked over one Aida square, both leaning the same way, to form an X. The default stitch of cross-stitch. Come up at bottom-left, down at top-right, up at bottom-right, down at top-left.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

content.text: variation where the first diagonal crosses two squares horizontally but only one square vertically. The return diagonal completes the cross by covering one square in each direction. The result is an asymmetric X that, when repeated in rows, locks into a braided or woven texture.

The stitch appears in traditional English and Scandinavian sampler borders and in filling patterns for background areas where the standard full cross would look too regular. Work it in two strands on 14-count
for the most visible braided texture.
How to work long arm cross-stitch in a row
Come up at the bottom-left hole of the first square. Work the long diagonal: go right two squares and up one square, down through the top-right hole of the second square.
Come up at the bottom-right hole of the first square (one square directly to the right of the start hole, on the same bottom row).

Work the short return diagonal: go left one square and up one square, down through the top-left hole of the second square (which is also the top-right hole of the first square). This completes the asymmetric cross.

Begin the next long arm cross by coming up at the bottom-right hole of the second square and repeating the sequence. In a continuous row the stitches share their entry and exit holes, which is what produces the plaited surface.

items.symptom: The stitches look like irregular full crosses rather than an even braid
items.cause: The long and short diagonals have been mixed up, or the row is not worked consistently left to right.
items.fix: Always work the long arm first (two squares across, one up), then the short return (one square back, one up). Work all stitches in a row in the same direction.

items.symptom: The row does not cover the fabric evenly and gaps show
items.cause: Stitches are not sharing their holes correctly with their neighbours.
items.fix: Check that the exit hole of the return diagonal of one stitch is the same as the entry hole of the long arm of the next stitch. They should share a hole.

content.text: Long arm cross-stitch is most at home as a sampler border, worked in a single colour to frame a central motif. Try a two-row border in a contrasting colour on any of the project tutorials in the quotes-and-sayings sub-category.
